messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load RL from a piezo harvester.
    *   Conditions:
        *   `vout_min`: $v_{avg} \ge 1.8$ V (Settled mean output).
        *   `vout_max`: $v_{max} \le 3.6$ V (Absolute maximum).
        *   `ripple`: $v_{pp} \le 0.05$ V (Peak-to-peak ripple).
        *   `startup`: $t_{up} \le 0.4$ s (Cold start time).
        *   `settled`: $dv \le 0.02$ V (Stability).
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25nF) and $R_{leak}$ (20M$\Omega$).
    *   Open circuit voltage: $V_{oc} \approx 3.2$ V (at nominal). This is quite low, so diode drops (DSCH ~0.25V) are significant.
    *   Load range: $150\text{k}\Omega$ (heavy) to $2200\text{k}\Omega$ (light).
    *   Voltage regulation is critical: must stay between 1.8V and 3.6V.

    *   FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) failed because:
        *   S2 (heavy load) failed $v_{out\_min}$ (not enough power).
        *   S3 (strong excitation, light load) failed $v_{out\_max}$ and $v_{pp}$ (overvoltage, too much ripple).
        *   S4 (weak excitation) failed $v_{out\_min}$ and $t_{up}$ (not enough power, too slow).
        *   S5 (low frequency) failed `settled` (stability/ripple).
    *   Conclusion: FBR lacks voltage regulation and cannot efficiently extract power from the piezo when $V_{oc}$ is low.

    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* Increases power extraction by flipping the piezo voltage.
    *   *Voltage Regulation:* A Zener clamp (DZ33) can prevent $v_{max}$ exceeding 3.6V, though 3.3V is the breakdown.
    *   *Storage:* A large capacitor on `out` is needed to reduce ripple.
    *   *Synchronous Rectification:* Replacing diodes with switches (SYNC) can reduce voltage drops.

    *   **Proposal 1: SSHI (Parallel-SSHI or Basic SSHI).**
        *   Topology: Inductor L and switch S across the piezo to flip voltage at extrema.
        *   Rectification: Full bridge (DSCH) to charge `out`.
        *   Regulation: Zener clamp on `out` to cap at 3.3V.
        *   Logic: SYNC controller flips the voltage at both peaks.
        *   *Wait*, a standard SSHI usually has the inductor flipping the piezo voltage *before* rectification.
        *   Circuit: Piezo $\to$ Full Bridge $\to$ C_out. Inductor and Switch across piezo.
        *   Wait, if I put the inductor and switch in parallel with the piezo, I can invert the charge.

    *   **Proposal 2: Synchronous Rectifier (Active Rectification).**
        *   Instead of diodes, use switches. However, the available `SYNC` controller is designed for "ton" pulses at extrema, which is more for SSHI (switching) than for continuous rectification (which requires phase-shifted 50% duty cycles).
        *   Let's stick to SSHI for power boost and Zener for regulation.

    *   **Proposal 3: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction).**
        *   A more advanced version of SSHI.
        *   Typically involves an inductor and switch that connects the piezo to the storage cap only at the peak.
        *   Structure: Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Diode $\to$ Out.
        *   This extracts energy more efficiently.

    *   *SSHI-like Power Boost:*
        *   Inductor $L_1$ and Switch $S_1$ in parallel with the piezo (between `pzp` and `pzn`).
        *   Full bridge diodes (DSCH) from piezo to `out`.
        *   Zener diode (DZ33) from `out` to `0`.
        *   Storage capacitor $C_{out}$ on `out`.
        *   `SYNC` controller $G_1$ closes $S_1$ at both edges. $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        *   This should increase $v_{avg}$ for S2/S4.

    *   *SECE-like Extraction:*
        *   Piezo terminals `pzp`/`pzn` are essentially a capacitor $C_p$ being charged by $I_p$.
        *   At the peak, we want to transfer this charge to `out`.
        *   Circuit: `pzp` $\to$ Switch $S_1$ $\to$ Inductor $L_1$ $\to$ Diode $D_1$ $\to$ `out`.
        *   (And another for the negative cycle: `pzn` $\to$ Switch $S_2$ $\to$ Inductor $L_2$ $\to$ Diode $D_2$ $\to$ `out`).
        *   Wait, the SYNC controller can handle "both" edges. If $S_1$ is connected between `pzp` and a node `n1`, and `n1` goes to $L_1$ then to `out` via $D_1$. If $S_2$ is connected between `pzn` and `n2`, and `n2` goes to $L_2$ then to `out` via $D_2$.
        *   This is basically a "synchronous charge extraction" circuit.

    *   *Refining Proposal 1 (SSHI):*
        *   Components:
            *   D1: [pzp, out], DSCH
            *   D2: [pzn, out], DSCH
            *   D3: [0, pzp], DSCH
            *   D4: [0, pzn], DSCH
            *   C_out: [out, 0], 2.2uF
            *   D_zener: [0, out], DZ33
            *   L1: [pzp, n1], 10mH
            *   S1: [n1, pzn], ctrl: G1
            *   G1: SYNC, edges: both, ton: 30us
        *   Wait, the standard SSHI inductor is across the piezo. The full bridge is then connected to the piezo terminals. This flips the voltage $V_{pzp}$ across the bridge.

    *   *Refining Proposal 2 (Simplified SECE/Synchronous Transfer):*
        *   S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        *   S2: [pzn, n2], ctrl: G1
        *   L1: [n1, n3], 10mH
        *   L2: [n2, n3], 10mH
        *   D1: [n3, out], DSCH
        *   C_out: [out, 0], 2.2uF
        *   D_zener: [0, out], DZ33
        *   G1: SYNC, edges: both.
        *   Actually, let's try a simpler approach. If we use `edges: both`, the switch closes every half period. If the switch is in parallel with the piezo, it's SSHI. If the switch is in series with an inductor and diode, it's SECE.

    *   *Alternative: Half-Bridge / Buck-Boost style?* No, the SYNC is very specific.

    *   Let's provide three variations:
        1.  **SSHI + Zener**: Classical SSHI to boost power, Zener to clamp voltage.
        2.  **SECE-like**: Transfer energy at peaks using L-D.
        3.  **Synchronous Bridge**: (Wait, I can't do a full synchronous bridge with only 2 SYNC controllers and fixed "ton" pulses). Let's do a modified SSHI with a different L placement.

    *   *Detailed SSHI (Design 1):*
        *   Piezo $\to$ Full Bridge $\to$ `out`.
        *   L1 and S1 in parallel with Piezo (pzp to pzn).
        *   Zener on `out`.
        *   C_out on `out`.
        *   Rationale: SSHI increases voltage extraction efficiency (fixes S2, S4). Zener prevents overvoltage (fixes S3). C_out reduces ripple (fixes S3, S5).

    *   *Detailed SECE (Design 2):*
        *   S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        *   S2: [pzn, n2], ctrl: G2
        *   L1: [n1, out], 10mH
        *   L2: [n2, out], 10mH
        *   D1: [out, n1], DSCH (Wait, the diode should be from L to out).
        *   Correct SECE:
            S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1 (edges: pos)
            L1: [n1, n2], 10mH
            D1: [n2, out], DSCH
            S2: [pzn, n3], ctrl: G2 (edges: neg)
            L2: [n3, n4], 10mH
            D2: [n4, out], DSCH
            C_out: [out, 0]
            DZ: [0, out], DZ33
        *   Rationale: SECE is generally more efficient than SSHI for low $V_{oc}$.

    *   *Detailed Hybrid (Design 3):*
        *   Try a simpler version of SSHI: Inductor $L_1$ between `pzp` and `n1`, switch $S_1$ between `n1` and `pzn`. This is just a series L-S.
        *   Wait, let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" (P-SSHI) variant. P-SSHI uses an auxiliary capacitor.
        *   P-SSHI:
            L1, S1 in parallel with an auxiliary cap $C_{aux}$.
            Then $C_{aux}$ is rectified to `out`.
            This is getting complex. Let's stick to a robust SSHI and SECE.

    *   Actually, for Design 3, let's try a "Charge Pump" or a different rectifier. Maybe a bridge with a lower drop? No, DSCH is already the lowest.
    *   How about a "Half-bridge" SSHI?
        *   S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        *   L1: [n1, pzn], 10mH
        *   D1: [pzp, out], DSCH
        *   D2: [pzn, out], DSCH
        *   D3: [0, pzp], DSCH
        *   D4: [0, pzn], DSCH
        *   Wait, that's just SSHI.

    *   Let's go with:
        1.  `sshi_zener`: SSHI inductor/switch across piezo, full bridge, zener clamp.
        2.  `sece_zener`: SECE inductors/switches, zener clamp.
        3.  `sshi_low_c`: Similar to SSHI but optimized for different $C_{out}$. (No, the optimizer does that). Let's try a "Half-Wave SSHI" (only one edge) to see if it helps stability.

    *   *Wait, reconsidering SECE (Design 2):*
        The SYNC controller can do "both" edges.
        If $S_1$ is [pzp, n1] and $S_2$ is [pzn, n1] (both controlled by G1, edges: both), then:
        When $pzp$ is peak, $S_1$ closes $\to$ $L_1$ from $n1$ to $out$.
        When $pzn$ is peak, $S_2$ closes $\to$ $L_1$ from $n1$ to $out$.
        This uses one inductor for both halves.
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G1
        L1: [n1, n2], 10mH
        D1: [n2, out], DSCH
        C_out: [out, 0]
        DZ: [0, out], DZ33
        G1: edges: both, ton: 30us.
        This is a very efficient way to transfer charge.

    *   Let's double-check the `S1` and `S2` constraints. "at most 4 switches". "at most 2 SYNC".
    *   Design 1 (SSHI):
        D1: [pzp, out], DSCH
        D2: [pzn, out], DSCH
        D3: [0, pzp], DSCH
        D4: [0, pzn], DSCH
        C1: [out, 0], 2.2uF
        D5: [0, out], DZ33
        L1: [pzp, n1], 10mH
        S1: [n1, pzn], ctrl: G1
        G1: SYNC, edges: both, ton: 30us, phase: 0
    *   Design 2 (SECE-lite):
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G1
        L1: [n1, n2], 10mH
        D1: [n2, out], DSCH
        C1: [out, 0], 2.2uF
        D2: [0, out], DZ33
        G1: SYNC, edges: both, ton: 30us, phase: 0
    *   Design 3 (Full-Bridge with Zener and larger cap - purely passive but with regulation):
        D1: [pzp, out], DSCH
        D2: [pzn, out], DSCH
        D3: [0, pzp], DSCH
        D4: [0, pzn], DSCH
        C1: [out, 0], 10uF
        D5: [0, out], DZ33
        (Wait, this is just a regulated FBR. FBR failed S2 and S4. So we need the power boost of L).
        Let's instead try SSHI but with a different inductor placement.
        L1: [pzp, n1], S1: [n1, 0], ctrl: G1 (Wait, that's not SSHI).

    *   Let's refine Design 3: SSHI with "pos" edge only.
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1 (edges: pos)
        L1: [n1, pzn], 10mH
        (plus full bridge and zener).
        Maybe the "both" edges in SSHI creates too much ripple or instability? Let's see.

    *   Actually, let's try a "synchronous charge extraction" with two inductors (one for each polarity) to be safer.
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1 (edges: pos)
        L1: [n1, n2], 10mH
        D1: [n2, out], DSCH
        S2: [pzn, n3], ctrl: G1 (edges: neg)
        L2: [n3, n4], 10mH
        D2: [n4, out], DSCH
        (Wait, a single SYNC controller can't do "pos" and "neg" differently? No, it says "edges: both, pos, or neg". If I use one SYNC, it's one of those. If I want different behavior, I need two SYNCs).

    *   Revised Design 2:
        G1: SYNC, edges: pos
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        L1: [n1, n2], 10mH
        D1: [n2, out], DSCH
        G2: SYNC, edges: neg
        S2: [pzn, n3], ctrl: G2
        L2: [n3, n4], 10mH
        D2: [n4, out], DSCH
        C1: [out, 0], 2.2uF
        D3: [0, out], DZ33

    *   Let's re-check the "S1: [pzn, n1]" for Design 2 (the one-inductor version).
        If G1 is "both":
        - At positive peak: $S_1$ closes, current flows $pzp \to n1 \to L_1 \to D_1 \to out$.
        - At negative peak: $S_2$ closes, current flows $pzn \to n1 \to L_1 \to D_1 \to out$.
        This works perfectly and uses fewer components.

    *   So, the three proposals:
        1. `sshi_zener`: Inductor+Switch across piezo, full bridge, zener, cap.
        2. `sece_single_l`: One inductor, two switches (pzp, pzn), one diode, zener, cap.
        3. `sece_dual_l`: Two inductors, two switches, two diodes, zener, cap.

    *   *Self-Correction on Design 2 (sece_single_l):*
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G1
        L1: [n1, n2], 10mH
        D1: [n2, out], DSCH
        Wait, if $S_1$ and $S_2$ are both closed by $G_1$ (edges: "both"), then at the positive peak $S_1$ and $S_2$ are both closed. That would short $pzp$ and $pzn$.
        The SYNC controller closes "its switches". If $S_1$ and $S_2$ both have `ctrl: G1`, they both close at the same time.
        To avoid shorting the piezo, I need:
        G1: edges: pos, S1: [pzp, n1]
        G2: edges: neg, S2: [pzn, n1]
        Then they never close simultaneously.

    *   *Wait, look at the SYNC description again:*
        "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema... edges: 'both', 'pos', 'neg'".
        This means if G1 is "both", any switch $S_x$ linked to G1 will close at both the positive and negative peak.
        If I want $S_1$ to close at the positive peak and $S_2$ at the negative, I *must* use two different SYNC controllers.

    *   *Revised Proposal 2 (sece_dual_l):*
        G1: edges: pos
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        L1: [n1, n2], 10mH
        D1: [n2, out], DSCH
        G2: edges: neg
        S2: [pzn, n3], ctrl: G2
        L2: [n3, n4], 10mH
        D2: [n4, out], DSCH
        C1: [out, 0], 2.2uF
        D3: [0, out], DZ33

    *   *Revised Proposal 1 (sshi_zener):*
        G1: edges: both
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        L1: [n1, pzn], 10mH
        D1: [pzp, out], DSCH
        D2: [pzn, out], DSCH
        D3: [0, pzp], DSCH
        D4: [0, pzn], DSCH
        C1: [out, 0], 2.2uF
        D5: [0, out], DZ33

    *   *Revised Proposal 3 (sece_single_l_dual_sync):*
        G1: edges: pos
        S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1
        G2: edges: neg
        S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G2
        L1: [n1, n2], 10mH
        D1: [n2, out], DSCH
        C1: [out, 0], 2.2uF
        D2: [0, out], DZ33

    *   *One last check on the SSHI (Design 1):*
        Is the inductor-switch across the piezo?
        S1: [n1, pzn], L1: [pzp, n1]. Yes, that's in parallel with the piezo.
        Wait, if the inductor and switch are in parallel with the piezo, and the full bridge is also in parallel, what happens?
        At the peak, the switch $S_1$ closes, $L_1$ resonates with $C_p$, flipping the voltage. The bridge then rectifies this flipped voltage. This is the standard SSHI.

    *   *Wait, in SSHI, the bridge is usually AFTER the flipping.*
        Piezo $\to$ L/S (parallel) $\to$ Bridge $\to$ Out.
        This is exactly what I have.
        Wait, if the L/S is in parallel with the piezo, the bridge is also in parallel with the piezo. So the bridge sees the flipped voltage. Correct.
